parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a dispatcher. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through a typical shift for you, from the moment you sit down at your desk to when you hand over and leave?
I don't know.
To start small, which of the drone operating companies do you work for, and what is the very first thing you do when you log in each day?
I don't know.
Thinking about the last drone flight you dealt with, what was your involvement in it?

I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, meaning I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can also call off a flight. However, I know nothing about software and accounts and passwords inside the service are not used since staff accounts are issued by the platform company outside it.
How does a request for a flight first reach you, and who does it come from?
I don't know.
When you are deciding which drone flies along which way, what information do you look at to make that decision?

I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts, but our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us. I can also call off a flight.
How do you work out today which of your drones could get to where a job starts?

I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. However, our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us, and choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility.
What details about a drone or a job do you need to see to tell if that drone can reach where the job starts?
I don't know.
Before you sign off a flight to leave, what do you check by hand because you don't trust anyone or anything else to get it right?
I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can call off a flight, and it is my legal responsibility to choose the drone and the way it flies.
What makes you decide to call off a flight?
I don't know.
Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day on the job, and what made it so bad?

I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and about closures coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on, and batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.
When a drone restarts in flight or radio coverage drops out, what happens on your end, and what do you need to know right after it comes back?

I worry about radio coverage being patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and about reports from drones arriving late, out of order, more than once, or not at all through relay stations. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.
When a closure comes into force while drones are already in the air, how do you find out about it, and what do you have to do right away?

I worry that a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.
When a sudden closure applies at once or an area is widened, how do you check if any of your drones are affected?
I don't know.
